# Filtering makes assumptions visible {background-color="#0C234B"}

## A mask is a labelled boolean sequence

```python
deep = wells["well_depth_ft"] > 500
deep_wells = wells.loc[deep].copy()
```

```python
northwest = wells.loc[
    (wells["latitude"] > 32.3)
    & (wells["longitude"] < -111.0)
].copy()
```

::: {.incremental}
- `&` means and; `|` means or; `~` means not
- each condition needs parentheses
- `.copy()` makes an intentional, independent subset
:::

## Missing values leave quietly

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 8
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
s = pd.Series([61.0, np.nan, 835.0])
print(s > 500)
print(f"kept {(s > 500).sum()} of {len(s)} rows")
```

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
Every comparison with `NaN` is `False`. Inspect missingness before filtering or
you will not know which records vanished.
:::

## Your turn: shallow northwest wells

Keep wells north of 32.3°, west of −111.0°, and shallower than 200 ft.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_filter
import pandas as pd
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "site": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"],
    "latitude": [32.35, 32.10, 32.41, 32.38, 32.05],
    "longitude": [-111.05, -110.90, -111.12, -110.85, -111.20],
    "depth_ft": [150.0, 90.0, 180.0, 120.0, 60.0],
})
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_filter
selected = wells.loc[______].copy()
print(selected)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Join three parenthesised comparisons with `&`. Western longitudes are negative.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_filter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
selected = wells.loc[
    (wells["latitude"] > 32.3)
    & (wells["longitude"] < -111.0)
    & (wells["depth_ft"] < 200)
].copy()
```

Wells A and C meet all three conditions.
:::
:::

## New columns should say what changed

```python
one_site["decline_ft"] = (
    one_site["depth_to_water_ft"]
    - one_site["depth_to_water_ft"].iloc[0]
)

levels["water_year"] = (
    levels["date"].dt.year
    + (levels["date"].dt.month >= 10)
)
```

::: {.fragment}
Depth increases downward, so positive `decline_ft` means a falling water table.
Names and units should make that convention explicit.
:::

# Grouping asks the same question repeatedly {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Split, apply, combine

```python
levels.groupby("site_no")["depth_to_water_ft"].mean()
levels.groupby("water_year")["depth_to_water_ft"].median()
levels.groupby(["site_no", "water_year"])["depth_to_water_ft"].mean()
```

::: {.fragment}
The important decision is the key: by site, year, month, aquifer, or a category
you computed.
:::

## `.agg()` names several summaries

```python
site_summary = levels.groupby("site_no")["depth_to_water_ft"].agg(
    n="size",
    first="first",
    last="last",
    shallowest="min",
    deepest="max",
)
```

::: {.fragment}
Named outputs produce a readable table in one pass. Sort by date before asking
for `first` or `last`.
:::

## Your turn: monthly climatology

Average all Januaries together, all Februaries together, and so on. Keep the
sample count beside the mean.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_group
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-03", "2020-01-20", "2020-02-05",
                        "2021-01-07", "2021-02-12", "2021-02-28"])
flow = pd.DataFrame({"discharge_cfs": [4, 8, 12, 10, 18, 24]}, index=dates)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_group
climatology = flow.groupby(______)["discharge_cfs"].agg(
    mean="mean", n="size"
)
print(climatology)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_group"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The month number is available from `flow.index.month`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_group"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
climatology = flow.groupby(flow.index.month)["discharge_cfs"].agg(
    mean="mean", n="size"
)
```

`groupby(month)` collapses across years. `resample("ME")` would retain every
separate month in chronological order.
:::
:::

# Rolling windows preserve the daily axis {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Resample or roll?

```python
monthly = q.resample("ME").mean()
rolling_30 = q.rolling(30, center=True).mean()
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Resample**

Fewer values at a new temporal resolution.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Rolling**

One smoothed value at nearly every original date.
:::
:::

## A centred window has honest missing ends

```python
rolling_30 = q.rolling(30, center=True).mean()
```

::: {.fragment}
The first and last 15 days are missing because half the window lies outside the
record.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
With `center=False`, each mean is labelled at the end of its window. That is
appropriate for forecasting from the past, but it shifts historical features
later by half a window.
:::

## Your turn: wettest sustained month

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_roll
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
idx = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=400, freq="D")
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(400) / 58)) * 40
              + rng.gamma(1, 3, 400), index=idx)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_roll
rolling_30 = q.rolling(______, center=______).mean()
wettest_date = ______
print(wettest_date, rolling_30.max())
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_roll"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Use a 30-day centred window. `.idxmax()` returns the date of the maximum.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_roll"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
rolling_30 = q.rolling(30, center=True).mean()
wettest_date = rolling_30.idxmax()
```

A high daily maximum describes a flood. A high 30-day mean describes sustained
wet conditions. They are not interchangeable statistics.
:::
:::

# Reshape for the next operation {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Long and wide store the same observations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Long**

```text
site  date        depth
A     2019-04-02   86.4
A     2020-03-18   88.1
B     2019-04-02   41.2
```

Compact; natural for filtering and grouping.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Wide**

```text
date         A      B
2019-04-02  86.4   41.2
2020-03-18  88.1    NaN
```

Convenient for comparing aligned series.
:::
:::

## Pivot deliberately

```python
wide = levels.pivot_table(
    index="date",
    columns="site_no",
    values="depth_to_water_ft",
)
```

::: {.fragment}
Irregular field visits make the wide table sparse. Stay long until a plot,
matrix operation, or aligned comparison actually needs wide data.
:::

::: {.fragment}
`pivot_table` averages duplicate site-date pairs. Check duplicates first or use
`pivot`, which raises rather than hiding them.
:::

## Your turn: reshape and count missing cells

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_pivot
import pandas as pd
long = pd.DataFrame({
    "site_no": ["A", "A", "B", "B", "C"],
    "date": pd.to_datetime(["2019-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2019-01-01",
                            "2021-01-01", "2020-01-01"]),
    "depth_ft": [31.0, 33.5, 88.0, 91.2, 55.0],
})
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_pivot
wide = long.pivot(index=______, columns=______, values="depth_ft")
n_empty = ______
print(wide)
print(n_empty)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_pivot"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Dates are rows and sites are columns. Sum the boolean missing-value table twice.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_pivot"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
wide = long.pivot(index="date", columns="site_no", values="depth_ft")
n_empty = wide.isna().sum().sum()
```

Five measurements occupy five of nine possible cells; four are missing.
:::
:::

## A first time-series plot is a diagnostic

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(one_site.index, one_site["depth_to_water_ft"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylabel("depth to water (ft below land surface)")
```

::: {.fragment}
When the quantity counts downward, the axis should too. Week 8 turns this
working plot into a figure worth showing people.
:::
